blocks.text: Imagine a world where every program believes it has access to a large, continuous block of memory. How is this illusion maintained in a computer system with limited physical memory?

blocks.markdown: In modern operating systems, memory management is crucial for providing each process with the illusion of having its own large, contiguous address space. This is achieved through a technique called **paging**. Paging divides the virtual address space of a process into fixed-size blocks called **pages**, which are mapped to physical memory frames.

blocks.title: Page
blocks.text: A page is a fixed-length contiguous block of virtual memory, which is the smallest unit of data for memory management in a virtual memory system.

blocks.markdown: The operating system maintains a **page table** for each process, which maps virtual pages to physical frames. When a process accesses a memory location, the virtual address must be translated into a physical address using this page table.

blocks.latex: Physical\ Address = Page\ Frame\ Number \times Page\ Size + Offset
blocks.caption: Formula for translating a virtual address to a physical address.

blocks.title: Translating a Virtual Address
blocks.prompt: Translate the virtual address 0x1C3 in a system with a page size of 256 bytes, where the page table maps virtual page 1 to physical frame 5.

steps.text: Convert the virtual address to binary: 0x1C3 = 0001 1100 0011.
Determine the page number and offset. With a page size of 256 bytes, the offset is the lower 8 bits: 0011 (3 in decimal). The page number is the remaining bits: 0001 (1 in decimal).
Look up the page number in the page table. Virtual page 1 maps to physical frame 5.
Calculate the physical address: Physical Address = 5 * 256 + 3 = 1283.

blocks.markdown: To speed up address translation, modern CPUs use a cache called the **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)**. The TLB stores a small number of recent page table entries, allowing for faster access.

blocks.title: TLB Miss
blocks.text: A TLB miss occurs when the required page table entry is not found in the TLB, necessitating a slower lookup in the main page table.

blocks.markdown: In systems with large address spaces, single-level page tables can become very large. **Multi-level page tables** are used to reduce memory usage by breaking the page table into smaller parts, which are loaded into memory only when needed.

blocks.title: Understanding Multi-level Page Tables
blocks.prompt: Explain why multi-level page tables are more efficient than single-level page tables in a 64-bit address space.

steps.text: A single-level page table for a 64-bit address space would require 2^64 entries, which is impractically large.
Multi-level page tables divide the address space into smaller segments, allowing only the necessary parts of the page table to be loaded into memory.
This reduces the memory overhead and improves efficiency by loading only the required page table entries.

blocks.answer: Multi-level page tables reduce memory usage by loading only necessary parts of the page table, making them more efficient for large address spaces.

blocks.title: Page Table Size
blocks.text: Be cautious of the memory overhead caused by large page tables in systems with extensive address spaces.

points: Paging divides virtual memory into pages, mapped to physical frames via a page table.
The TLB speeds up address translation by caching recent page table entries.
Multi-level page tables reduce memory overhead in large address spaces.
